title: Cooking on the River: Episode 3
contentHtml:
In the final episode of the series, we perform Beethoven as a chamber trio, steam (and eat) smash burgers like they're sliders, and hitch a plane ride out of the canyon.

The finale of Cooking on the River is here! This episode concludes our epic culinary and musical journey down the Colorado River as part of the Moab Music Festival. After four days rafting, camping, hiking, and being a covered in a little dust for a lot of the time, we hitched a plane ride out of the canyon and were deposited back into real life.

A special thanks is due to the Moab Music Festival for hosting such a special occasion and to the river crew from Sheri Griffith River Expeditions for keeping us afloat and well fed.

I also need to thank my own crew: Lena Davidson, my head of operations and chef extraordinaire, who made this trip and the chaos of running mobile campsite kitchens manageable. Editor David Zimmermann (of Rebel Clef studios) who masterfully put together this docuseries for all of you to enjoy. And finally, for any Frienjis that joined us—either physically or virtually—on this adventure: Thank you, too! This trip is incredibly unique and it's been a true joy to share in it with you.

Recipes from the River: The Complete Menu

The theme of this trip—the inspiration behind the music and food choices that brought the journey to life—was This Land: Exploring how quintessentially American music and food grew from global exchange. We've been sharing our Recipes from the River over the past week, but wanted to recap the complete menu from the three-night journey.

Night One: Seattle-Style Teriyaki

Seattle-style teriyaki shows how Japanese culinary traditions were adapted by immigrant cooks into something distinctly American and distinctly Pacific Northwestern. We served this traditional Seattle meal—teriyaki chicken, steamed white rice, and teriyaki shop salad—alongside soy-butter corn and a melon and shiso salad on the side.

Night Two: Sichuan Shrimp and Grits

A deliberate collision of Southern and Sichuan traditions. Shrimp and grits is already a product of cultural exchange; here, creamy grits brings the comfort of congee doctored up with a stir-fry and flavorful toppings. For this meal, buttery grits were topped with stir-fried shrimp and mushrooms with fermented bean paste. On the side was a cucumber and red onion salad and braised green beans with pickled mustard greens (which make for a killer Thanksgiving side, too—recipe coming soon).

Night Three: Oklahoma Onion Burgers

Great Depression–era cooks at diners in El Reno, Oklahoma, stretched beef with inexpensive onions, and the workaround became a beloved technique in its own right that is more popular today than it’s ever been. We served these Oklahoma onion burgers with assorted toppings, a red cabbage-dill slaw, and a Japanese potato salad using any leftover ingredients we had on the last night of the journey.

Thanks again for following along with this series—we hope you enjoyed! You can watch all episodes, and find all the recipes from the river, in the collection right here on Patreon.
